title: ARE WE FUNDING THE GREAT COMMISSION… OR BUILDING EMPIRES AROUND RELIGIOUS CELEBRITIES?
paragraphs: ARE WE FUNDING THE GREAT COMMISSION… OR BUILDING EMPIRES AROUND RELIGIOUS CELEBRITIES?
Jesus Never Asked Us to Make Preachers Famous. He Commanded Us to Make Disciples. Somewhere Between the Cross and the Spotlight, Have We Forgotten Who the Church Belongs To?
What if the most frightening thing about modern Christianity isn't that the world has stopped listening to the Church…
But that parts of the Church have become so fascinated with their own success that they've stopped listening to Jesus?
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, a missionary is wondering how to afford another month of ministry.
Somewhere, a small congregation is struggling to keep its doors open.
Somewhere, a Christian mother is praying over an almost-empty refrigerator while trying to teach her children that God is faithful.
And somewhere else, under dazzling lights, surrounded by cameras, expensive equipment, and thunderous applause, a preacher is being celebrated like the very Savior he was supposed to proclaim.
The crowd is enormous.
The production is breathtaking.
The branding is flawless.
But one question hangs over everything.
If Jesus walked into the room without announcing His name, would we recognize Him… or would we ask Him to move because He was blocking the camera?
That question should disturb us.

Not because every large ministry is corrupt. Not because excellence is sinful. Not because pastors should live in poverty or because Christians should be ashamed of supporting those who preach the Gospel.
Scripture teaches otherwise.
But because there is a dangerous difference between using resources to make Jesus known and using Jesus' name to make ourselves important.
And the frightening part?
That difference can disappear so gradually that even sincere believers may not notice.
Until the applause becomes louder than the Gospel.
Until the personality becomes more important than the message.
Until financial success becomes the evidence of God's approval.
Until the cross becomes part of the branding rather than the reason for everything.
And perhaps the hardest question isn't what the celebrity preacher is doing with the money.
Perhaps it's what we have trained ourselves to admire.
Because we can condemn the golden calf while still helping to build one.
Remember what happened at the foot of Mount Sinai?
The Israelites had witnessed the power of God. They had seen deliverance from Egypt. They had walked through the sea. They had received mercy they could never have purchased.
Yet while Moses was on the mountain, they fashioned a golden calf.
They took valuable things and created something visible, impressive, and religiously significant.
Then they worshiped it.
Exodus 32:4 records Aaron's declaration identifying the calf with the gods who had brought Israel out of Egypt.
Think about the tragedy.
They were attributing God's saving work to something their own hands had made.

And although today's churches are not automatically guilty of Israel's ancient idolatry simply because they have beautiful buildings, large audiences, or sophisticated ministries, the spiritual warning remains painfully relevant.
Anything that receives the devotion, trust, or glory belonging to God alone can become an idol—even when it stands inside a religious building.
A platform can become an idol.
A ministry name can become an idol.
A pastor's reputation can become an idol.
Even a successful Christian movement can become an idol when protecting the institution becomes more important than obeying Christ.
And the people most vulnerable to this deception are not necessarily those who hate Jesus.
Sometimes they are those who sincerely love Him but have slowly confused admiration for a spiritual leader with devotion to their Lord.
That is why we need to return to something Jesus said that modern religious culture cannot afford to ignore.
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus confronted the disciples' understanding of greatness.
The Greek text of Mark 10:43 includes the words:
μέγας γενέσθαι ἐν ὑμῖν… ἔσται ὑμῶν διάκονος
megas genesthai en hymin… estai hymōn diakonos
The meaning is that whoever desires to become great among them must become their servant.
The word διάκονος (diakonos) refers to a servant or minister—someone whose role is to serve rather than dominate.
And Jesus went further.
Mark 10:45, in the King James Version, declares:
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."
There it is.
The King of kings defined greatness through service.
The Lord of glory described His mission through sacrifice.
The One before whom every knee will bow did not build His earthly ministry around demanding celebrity treatment.
He washed feet.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed children.
He ate with sinners.
He approached the broken.
He carried the cross.
And He gave His life for people who could never repay Him.
How, then, did we arrive at a place where some expressions of Christian leadership seem more concerned with being treated like royalty than following the Servant King?
How did we begin confusing extravagance with anointing?
How did popularity become a substitute for spiritual maturity?
How did some believers learn to defend a preacher's lifestyle more passionately than they defend the character of Christ?
Before we point fingers, however, we need to examine our own hearts.
Because religious celebrity culture does not survive on charismatic leaders alone.
It also survives on audiences that sometimes prefer being impressed to being discipled.
We love powerful voices.
We love dramatic moments.
We love stories of extraordinary success.
We love being associated with something big.
And none of those things is automatically sinful.
But when the sermon ends, do we know Jesus more deeply?
Are we becoming more honest?
More generous?
More compassionate?
More willing to repent?
More faithful in private?
More committed to Scripture?
Or have we simply become more emotionally attached to the person holding the microphone?
Paul confronted this danger in Corinth.
Some believers were dividing themselves around prominent Christian workers, identifying with Paul, Apollos, or Cephas.
In 1 Corinthians 1:13, Paul asked:
"Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?"
That question still cuts through the noise.
Was your favorite preacher crucified for you?
Did your preferred ministry founder rise from the grave for your justification?
Did the personality you defend so fiercely shed sinless blood to reconcile you to God?
No.
Jesus did.
And if a ministry has become so centered on one human personality that believers can barely imagine following Christ without that personality, something has gone terribly wrong.
The Church is not the bride of a preacher.
The Church is the bride of Christ.
And no servant, however gifted, has the right to take the Bridegroom's place.
Now consider another scene.
Jesus is sitting near the temple treasury.
People are bringing their offerings.
The wealthy are giving large amounts.
Then a poor widow approaches.
She contributes two small coins.
To human eyes, her gift seems insignificant.
But Jesus sees what everyone else overlooks.
Mark 12:43–44 records His observation that she gave more, proportionally, than those contributing from their abundance, because she gave from her poverty.
This passage is often used to encourage sacrificial giving.
But we must handle it carefully.
Immediately before this scene, Jesus warned against religious leaders who "devour widows' houses" (Mark 12:40).
And immediately afterward, He foretold the destruction of the temple buildings (Mark 13:1–2).
The surrounding context raises a sobering concern about religious leadership and the vulnerable.
Jesus truly recognized the widow's extraordinary sacrifice.
But the passage does not give religious institutions permission to pressure impoverished people into surrendering money they need for survival.
It certainly does not authorize a preacher to exploit someone's desperation by promising a miracle in exchange for a donation.
God sees the widow.
God also sees anyone who takes advantage of her.

And if our fundraising strategies leave struggling believers feeling that God will love them less unless they give beyond their means, we need to ask whether we are reflecting the heart of Jesus at all.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
Grace is not a premium product.
Forgiveness is not unlocked by a financial transaction.
And the Holy Spirit cannot be purchased.
Acts 8:18–23 tells us what happened when Simon attempted to obtain spiritual power through money.
Peter rebuked him severely.
The lesson remains unmistakable.
The gifts of God are not merchandise.
And the people of God must never be treated as customers whose spiritual worth is measured by their ability to pay.
Yet we must also be careful not to swing toward another unbiblical extreme.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not wrong.
It is deeply biblical.
In fact, faithful financial partnership has helped spread the message of Christ across generations.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 9:14:
"Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel."
In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul acknowledged the Philippian believers' material partnership in his ministry.
Their generosity mattered.
Their gifts supported real Gospel work.
Their participation reflected genuine love.
And Paul described their offering in language associated with worship and sacrifice pleasing to God.
This means Christians do not need to apologize for supporting faithful pastors, missionaries, teachers, evangelists, and ministries.
Workers deserve appropriate support.
Churches require resources.
Missionaries need food, transportation, shelter, training, and practical assistance.
Discipleship resources cost money to prepare and distribute.
Digital evangelism requires infrastructure.
And a ministry can use modern technology, quality production, professional equipment, and effective communication without betraying Christ.
The question is not whether ministry costs money.
The question is whether money is serving the mission—or the mission has become an excuse for accumulating money.
That distinction changes everything.
A beautiful church building is not necessarily a monument to pride.
But it becomes spiritually dangerous when maintaining its image matters more than caring for people.
A pastor receiving a reasonable salary is not exploiting the flock.
But a pastor using spiritual authority to demand luxury, silence legitimate questions, or enrich himself through manipulation must be held accountable.
A ministry with millions of followers is not necessarily compromised.
But millions of followers cannot prove that its teaching is faithful.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:21–23 that impressive religious activity is not the same as genuinely belonging to Him.
The final measure of faithfulness is not audience size.
It is not revenue.
It is not influence.
It is not a verified account.
It is whether we truly know Christ, obey His Word, and bear the fruit of a life transformed by grace.
And this brings us to a question that deserves more attention than it receives.
Where does the money go?
Not as an accusation against every ministry.
Not as an excuse for cynicism.
But as a matter of biblical stewardship.
When Christians give, they are entrusting resources to people who must handle them faithfully.
Paul took financial integrity seriously.
In 2 Corinthians 8:20–21, he described precautions taken in administering a generous collection, emphasizing honorable conduct before God and people.
In other words, accountability was not an insult to ministry.
It was part of protecting ministry.
Transparent financial practices are not evidence of weak faith.
They are evidence that those entrusted with resources understand their responsibility.
A faithful ministry should not fear reasonable questions about how donations are used.
Are funds helping communicate the Gospel faithfully?
Are people being discipled?
Are the vulnerable being cared for?
Are resources being managed responsibly?
Are leaders accountable?
Are the people giving being treated with dignity rather than manipulated through fear, guilt, or exaggerated promises?
And perhaps most importantly…
If the founder's name disappeared tomorrow, would the ministry still have a reason to exist?
Because if everything collapses when the celebrity disappears, we may have built more around a personality than around the unchanging Gospel.
John the Baptist understood this.
He had a remarkable ministry.
Crowds came to hear him.
People responded to his preaching.
He had influence.
He had disciples.
Yet when Jesus emerged, John did not compete for attention.
He said something that should be written above every Christian pulpit, every ministry office, every broadcasting studio, and every social media account bearing the name of Christ.
John 3:30:
"He must increase, but I must decrease."
The Greek reads:
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
ekeinon dei auxanein, eme de elattousthai.
A faithful rendering is:
"He must increase, but I must decrease."
The word δεῖ (dei) conveys necessity.
John was not merely expressing a personal preference.
He recognized the necessity of Christ's increasing prominence and his own diminishing role.
And this was not self-hatred.
It was spiritual clarity.
John knew he was not the Messiah.
He was a witness.
A voice.
A servant preparing the way.
What freedom there is in remembering that!
We do not have to be the center of the story.
We do not have to be indispensable.
We do not have to build a personal empire to prove that God is using us.
We simply have to be faithful to the One who called us.
Imagine what would happen if every Christian leader sincerely prayed:

"Lord, if my influence grows, let Your truth become clearer. If my ministry expands, let my humility deepen. If resources increase, let generosity increase with them. And if You ever need to remove my name from the spotlight so people can see Yours, give me the grace to step aside."
That is a dangerous prayer.
Dangerous to pride.
Dangerous to vanity.
Dangerous to the craving for recognition.
But beautiful in the sight of a Savior who wore a crown of thorns.
And perhaps this is where the conversation becomes deeply personal.
Because you may be reading this after having been disappointed by a Christian leader.
Maybe you trusted someone who seemed sincere.
You listened to the sermons.
You defended the ministry.
You gave what you could.
You invited friends.
You believed the promises.
Then something happened.
A scandal.
A financial controversy.
A betrayal.
An abuse of authority.
Or simply the slow realization that the person you admired was not who you thought they were.
And suddenly, your faith felt shaken.
Not necessarily because Jesus failed you.
But because someone who claimed to represent Him did.
If that is your story, please hear this carefully.
The failure of a Christian leader does not mean the Gospel has failed.
Jesus never promised that every person speaking His name would faithfully represent His heart.
In fact, He warned us about false prophets and deceptive religious appearances.
Your grief is real.
Your disappointment matters.
Questions about wrongdoing should not be dismissed as rebellion.
And forgiveness does not require pretending that harm never occurred or abandoning appropriate accountability.
But do not allow someone else's unfaithfulness to convince you that Christ Himself is unfaithful.
The Savior who exposed religious hypocrisy is not embarrassed by your honest questions.
He is not threatened by the truth.
He is not dependent on the reputation of any human institution.
And He does not need us to conceal evil in order to protect His name.
Remember the temple courts.
In Mark 11:15–17, Jesus confronted commercial activity and wrongdoing in the temple precincts.
He overturned the tables of the money changers.
He challenged the corruption of a place intended for prayer.
And He cited Scripture concerning God's house being a house of prayer for all nations.
The context concerns the temple and its sacred purpose, not a simplistic condemnation of every financial transaction connected with modern Christian ministry.
Still, the event reveals something essential about Christ's character.
Jesus was not indifferent when religious activity obscured worship and justice.
He confronted it.
And His holiness was not the opposite of His love.
It was part of His love.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners also rebuked hypocrisy.
The same Jesus who forgave the repentant also warned those who exploited others.
The same Jesus who healed the wounded also called people to turn away from sin.
Grace does not mean truth becomes optional.
And accountability does not mean mercy disappears.
The Gospel holds both together.
Which is why the answer to religious celebrity culture is not to stop supporting every ministry.
It is to become more discerning about what we support.
Not every ministry with a large budget is corrupt.
Not every small ministry is faithful.
Not every well-known preacher is prideful.
Not every unknown preacher is humble.
We must judge teaching and conduct by Scripture rather than appearances.
And we must remember that even our own giving can become a way of seeking recognition.
Jesus addressed this in Matthew 6:1–4.
He warned against practicing acts of righteousness merely to be seen by others.
The point was not that generosity should never be publicly acknowledged.
The point was that the desire for human applause must not become the motive for giving.
God sees what is done in secret.
He sees the sacrifice nobody celebrates.
He sees the believer who quietly helps a struggling family.
He sees the widow whose small contribution represents real love.
He sees the missionary supporter who never appears on a stage.
He sees the person who shares a Scripture passage with one discouraged friend.
He sees the volunteer who serves when nobody is recording.
And He sees the believer who cannot afford to give money right now but faithfully offers prayer, encouragement, and service.
Your value in God's Kingdom is not determined by the size of your donation.
And your place in Christ's family is not reserved for financial supporters.
It is received by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakable.
Salvation is God's gift.
Not a reward we purchase.
Not a status we earn.
Not an achievement we can boast about.
And that truth must remain at the center of every ministry that calls itself Christian.
So what does this mean for Gospel Warrior?
It means we must be willing to apply the same biblical standard to ourselves that we ask others to follow.
We cannot challenge religious celebrity culture while secretly longing to build our own version of it.
We cannot preach generosity while treating people as financial targets.
We cannot speak about the Great Commission while forgetting the people Christ commissioned us to serve.
Our purpose must never be to make Gospel Warrior more important than Jesus.
Our purpose is to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, grow in their understanding of the Gospel, recognize sin, receive God's grace, and follow Christ more faithfully.
Because behind every view is a person.
Behind every share is a relationship.
Behind every comment may be a struggle nobody else knows about.
Think about what that can mean.
A new believer who has no idea where to begin studying Scripture can discover resources that help establish a foundation.
A struggling Christian who feels spiritually dry can find encouragement to return to God's Word.
A parent trying to raise children in the faith can discover material to support conversations about Jesus at home.
A believer recovering from disappointment can be reminded that discipleship is rooted in Christ rather than the perfection of human leaders.
And someone searching for answers may encounter biblical truth that invites them to examine the claims of the Gospel.
These resources are not substitutes for Scripture, prayer, faithful local church fellowship, or accountable pastoral care.
They are tools intended to support those things.
And keeping Christian resources freely accessible is part of the mission we want to preserve.
But free access does not mean producing, organizing, maintaining, and expanding ministry resources has no cost.
Behind meaningful digital discipleship are practical responsibilities.
Research.
Writing.
Editing.
Resource development.
Platform maintenance.
Content distribution.
Outreach.
And the ongoing work of making biblically grounded materials accessible to more people.
This is where faithful partnership can make a genuine difference.
Not because God will withhold His blessing if you don't.
But because voluntary, prayerful support can help sustain and expand the work you believe is worth sharing.
In the New Testament, believers partnered materially with Gospel workers because they wanted to participate in the mission.
That same principle can guide us today.

It should not automatically be described as replacing the biblical responsibility to support one's local church, nor should anyone be pressured to redirect giving that belongs to existing family, church, or charitable commitments.

The Bible's teaching on tithes and offerings deserves careful attention to covenant context. The New Testament particularly emphasizes willing, proportionate, generous giving rather than financial coercion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
A cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to participate.
Pray with us.
Read Scripture with us.
Grow with us.
Share the resources.
Encourage someone.
The Gospel must never become a members-only privilege.
But there is something else you can do that may cost you nothing and still matter greatly.
Not to advertise a personality.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass a pastor.
But to begin a conversation the Church urgently needs.
Someone may be giving money out of fear rather than faith.
Someone may have begun confusing a preacher's popularity with God's approval.
Someone may be struggling to trust Christian leadership again.
And someone may simply need to remember that the center of Christianity is not a celebrity, a platform, or an institution.
It is Jesus Christ.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, don't rush past that moment.
Maybe you have been too quick to idolize gifted leaders.
Maybe you have become cynical toward every ministry because of the failures of a few.
Maybe you have been reluctant to support any Gospel work because you fear being deceived again.
Maybe you have supported ministries for the wrong reasons.
Or maybe you are a Christian leader who has quietly begun measuring your worth by numbers, donations, followers, and applause.
There is grace for honest repentance.
There is wisdom for those willing to learn.
And there is freedom in returning to the One who never asked us to compete for His glory.
Or, if you are still healing from disappointment with religious leadership, you can simply comment, "Christ is still healing me."
You do not need to explain your pain publicly.
You do not owe strangers the details of your story.
But your honest response may remind another wounded believer that they are not alone.
And if you have witnessed faithful, humble Christian leadership, consider sharing that testimony too.
We need to recognize corruption without forgetting to honor integrity.
We need to confront exploitation without becoming incapable of gratitude.
We need to distinguish false teaching from faithful teaching.
And we need to remember that Jesus is still building His Church.
Yet before we finish, there is one final scene I want you to imagine.
Not a modern stage.
Not a megachurch auditorium.
Not a recording studio.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A place called Golgotha.
There are no luxury seats reserved for wealthy donors.
No elaborate promotional campaign.
No celebrity entrance.
No applause celebrating the One who is about to accomplish the greatest act of redemption in human history.
Instead, there is mockery.
Blood.
Shame.
Pain.
A crown made of thorns.
And the Son of God hanging between criminals.
The world sees a scandal.
Heaven's redemptive purpose is unfolding.
The innocent One is bearing the sins of the guilty.
The Shepherd is laying down His life for the sheep.
The Savior is accomplishing what no amount of human money, influence, religious performance, or personal success could ever accomplish.
He is making a way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
In John 19:30, Jesus declares:
Τετέλεσται.
Tetelestai.
"It is finished."
This Greek word comes from τελέω (teleō), meaning to finish, complete, or bring to fulfillment.
In the context of John's Gospel, Jesus' declaration announces the completion of the work entrusted to Him as He gives up His life.
It is not a marketing slogan.
It is not a promise that every earthly difficulty will immediately disappear.
It is the triumphant declaration of the crucified Savior who has faithfully completed His mission.
And on the third day, the tomb did not hold Him.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
The crucified Messiah is the risen Lord.
And because He lives, sinners can repent, receive forgiveness, and be made new through faith in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not a preacher becoming rich.
Not a ministry becoming famous.
Not a platform becoming influential.
Those things may be present or absent, and none of them can replace the saving work of Christ.
The Gospel is the good news of what God has accomplished through the death and resurrection of His Son.
And the Great Commission flows from that victory.
In Matthew 28:18–20, the risen Jesus commands His followers to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey everything He commanded.
The Greek phrase at the heart of Matthew 28:19 is:
μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
mathēteusate panta ta ethnē
"Make disciples of all nations."
The verb μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate) is an imperative calling Jesus' followers to make disciples.
Not merely admirers.
Not merely spectators.
Not merely consumers of religious content.
Disciples.
People who learn from Jesus, trust Him, obey Him, and grow in His likeness.
This is the mission worth funding.
This is the calling worth sacrificing for.
This is the purpose worth giving our time, talents, prayers, resources, and lives to advance.
And it belongs to Jesus.
Not to a celebrity.
Not to a brand.
Not even to Gospel Warrior.
To Jesus.
Does this draw people toward Christ?
Does it honor the truth of Scripture?
Does it encourage genuine discipleship?
Does it demonstrate integrity and accountability?
Does it serve people rather than merely impress them?
And am I giving freely, wisely, and lovingly rather than out of fear or pressure?
Because Christian generosity should not build golden calves.
It should serve the purposes of the living God.
Not to glorify us.
But to help us keep pointing beyond ourselves to Him.
Our commitment must always be that the Gospel remains greater than the platform, the truth greater than the personality, and Jesus greater than every name we might build for ourselves.
And if we ever forget that, may God give us the humility to repent.
Because one day the lights will go out.
The microphones will fall silent.
The algorithms will change.
The platforms we spent years building will pass away.
Our names may be forgotten.
Our accomplishments may fade.
And no number of followers will stand in our place before the throne of God.
But Jesus Christ will remain.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Savior who rose.
The King who reigns.
The One who takes sinners from shame into forgiveness, from rebellion into repentance, from spiritual death into new life.
And the question that will matter is not whether the world remembered our ministry.
It is whether our lives faithfully pointed people to Him.
Build whatever you must to reach the lost—but never build anything so high that the wounded can no longer see the cross.
